+# Rate limiter: switch from fixed-window counter to sliding window
+
+## What changed
+
+`createLimiter(limit, windowMs, now)` in `rate.js` now keeps a log of accepted-call timestamps per key, rather than a counter that resets at window boundaries. A call is allowed when fewer than `limit` accepted calls happened in the last `windowMs`.
+
+```
+allow(key):
+  recent = hits[key] minus timestamps where (t - x) >= windowMs
+  if recent.length >= limit -> store recent, return false   // rejected calls are not logged
+  else                      -> push t, store, return true
+```
+
+What callers will notice: a client can no longer send `limit` calls at the end of one window and another `limit` calls at the start of the next. The fixed window allowed up to 2×`limit` across a boundary. The sliding window allows at most `limit` in any `windowMs` span.
+
+## Where to look first
+
+1. **`rate.js:6`, the expiry comparison `t - x < windowMs`** (logic). A hit counts for `[x, x + windowMs)` and drops out exactly `windowMs` later. Check that this matches what callers expect at the boundary. The existing tests don't cover it (see Evidence).
+2. **`rate.js:3`, `hits` Map** (resources). Memory use changes from one counter per key to up to `limit` timestamps per key. Keys are never evicted, so a key that stops calling keeps its entry. With a large `limit` or many distinct keys (per-IP, for example), this grows without bound (measured below: +123 MB for 100k keys × limit 100, never released).
+3. **`rate.js:6`, `filter` on every call** (performance). Each call costs O(`limit`). That's fine for small limits but worth checking if `limit` is in the thousands.
+
+## Evidence
+
+Run on the current tree:
+
+- `node test.js` → `rate tests passed (4 assertions)` (exit 0).
+
+`test.js` doesn't tell the two algorithms apart: a fixed-window counter passes the same four assertions. To check the sliding behaviour I ran this one-off probe outside the suite (`limit=2`, `windowMs=1000`):
+
+| t (ms) | call | result | why |
+|---|---|---|---|
+| 0 | `k` | allowed | |
+| 900 | `k` | allowed | |
+| 1000 | `k` | allowed | hit at 0 is exactly `windowMs` old, so it has expired |
+| 1001 | `k` | **denied** | hits at 900 and 1000 are in the window. A fixed window starting at 1000 would have allowed this |
+| 1900 | `k` | allowed | hit at 900 has expired |
+| 1900 | `j` | allowed | keys are independent |
+
+Suggestion: add the t=900/1000/1001 case to `test.js` so a revert to a fixed window would fail the suite.
+
+**Compared with a fixed window.** The original fixed-window code isn't in the repo, so I compared the new limiter with a standard fixed-window counter written for this check (`limit=2`, `windowMs=1000`). The two disagree in both directions:
+
+| t (ms) | sliding | fixed |
+|---|---|---|
+| 1001 | denied | allowed |
+| 1900 | allowed | denied |
+
+Four calls in 2 ms across the boundary (t=999, 999, 1000, 1000): sliding allowed 2, fixed allowed 4.
+
+**Memory.** Node, measured with forced GC. 100,000 keys × `limit=100`, every slot filled: **+123 MB of heap**. The heap stays at +123 MB long after every window has expired, because nothing is freed until a key is called again. A fixed counter would need roughly one small object per key. For a per-IP limiter, add eviction (for example, a periodic sweep that deletes keys whose newest hit has expired) before or soon after merging.
+
+**Clock going backwards.** Two hits at t=5000, then the clock jumps back to t=1000. The key is **denied** until t=6000, because the "future" timestamps count as recent until the clock catches up. The limiter fails closed: a backward jump causes temporary over-rejection for keys that were near their limit, never over-admission.

+
+**Two-way door.** The exported API (`createLimiter(limit, windowMs, now)` → `allow(key)`) is unchanged and nothing is persisted, so a revert is a one-file change. +# Lesson: Never use float money in `src/billing`
+
+## Rule
+
+In `src/billing`, money is stored and computed as **integer cents**. Never represent amounts as floats, and never use `round()` on a float to "fix" a money value.
+
+## What happened
+
+In the March invoice run, an amount came out of float arithmetic as `10.299999`. Rounding the float didn't recover the right value: `npm run invoices` showed **10.29 instead of 10.30**, so the customer was billed a cent short.
+
+## Why
+
+Binary floats can't represent most decimal fractions exactly (e.g. `0.1`, `10.30`). Sums drift slightly above or below the true value. Rounding or formatting that drifted value can then land on the wrong cent. Integer cents stay exact.
+
+## Do / Don't
+
+| Don't | Do |
+|---|---|
+| `price = 10.30` | `price_cents = 1030` |
+| `round(sum(i["price"] for i in items), 2)` | `sum(i["price_cents"] for i in items)` |
+| Convert back and forth between floats and cents mid-calculation | Keep cents through the whole calculation; turn them into dollars only when formatting for display |
+| Parse user or CSV input with `float()` | Parse into cents with `Decimal` or string handling, e.g. `int(Decimal("10.30") * 100)` |
+
+If a calculation needs fractional cents (tax rates, proration), do it with `Decimal` and an explicit rounding mode (e.g. `ROUND_HALF_UP`), then convert to integer cents once.
+
+## Checklist for billing changes
+
+- [ ] No `float` amounts or float literals for money in the diff
+- [ ] No `round()` applied to money
+- [ ] Field names make the unit clear (`*_cents`)
+- [ ] There's a test where float math would drift, e.g. items that should sum to exactly 10.30
